lede: The same moments of 1071 in the eyewitness Attaleiates, the Seljuk-court historian Ibn al-Athīr, and the Armenian chronicler Matthew of Edessa. Each column shows the English; the reader carries the originals.

pairs.frage: Was the emperor embraced or beaten?
pairs.note: Attaleiates, who was not present at the meeting but wrote within a decade, has the sultan rise and embrace his captive; Ibn al-Athīr, a century and a half later, has three blows before the pardon; Matthew has chains and then brotherhood sealed in blood. All three keep the question 'What would you have done?', and the sultan's refusal to answer in kind.

pairs.frage: Who offered peace, and why was it refused?
pairs.note: All three have the sultan offer peace and the emperor refuse. Attaleiates blames advisers who said the sultan was playing for time; Ibn al-Athīr gives the emperor a boast ('no truce except at Rayy'); Matthew has the offer come after traitors had written to the sultan that half the army was his, and the refusal swell the emperor's pride.

pairs.frage: A general's plan or a traitor's plot?
pairs.note: Attaleiates defends the division at Theodosiopolis as a reasonable plan overturned by Providence, and says the blame others put on the emperor comes from ignorance. Matthew makes it the work of treacherous counsellors who wrote to the sultan when it was done.

pairs.frage: The Uzes, the Doukas reserve, or the officers who went home?
pairs.note: Attaleiates swore the Uzes in himself and says none of them went over in the battle; he reports 'as most people assert' that a cousin of the emperor's stepson spread the rumour of defeat. Matthew has the Uzes and Pechenegs go over in the thick of the fight, and Tarkhaniotes and the officers leave for Constantinople. Ibn al-Athīr sees one charge through the dust. The game follows Attaleiates and ties the rout of the reserve to the Doukai.

pairs.frage: What did the emperor promise, and who broke it?
pairs.note: Attaleiates names no sum; Ibn al-Athīr names one and a half million dinars, troops on demand and a fifty years' truce, and has the deposed emperor send what he could; Matthew has the sultan declare the peace broken by the blinding. The field made a treaty; the City undid it.

pairs.frage: Who did it, on whose order, and after what promise?
pairs.note: Attaleiates has the terms at Adana guaranteed by three bishops, an order from Michael VII, and the blinding done three times over at Kotyaion; Matthew of Edessa has Romanos put on the monk's habit himself to save his life, and the Romans 'crucify God a second time'; Ibn al-Athīr ends with the deposed emperor sending the sultan what money he had, and says nothing of the blinding. Both Christian writers lay the deed, in different figures, on the Jews: a commonplace carried here as printed and named as such.
